primitives.verbatim_quote: The data set was augmented with composite team ratings<sup>4</sup> for each recruiting class dating back to 2008 to account for seniors in the 2011 season.

primitives.name: Intuitive binary prediction fusion
primitives.verbatim_quote: Our decision rule was designed to be as intuitive as possible – if both predictions resulted in the same team being favored, the favored team was deemed the predicted winner.
primitives.assumptions: Assumes two independent predictive models; assumes equal weightage to each model's directionality; assumes no prior knowledge of model reliabilities.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Applies when only two models disagree on direction; breaks down if models have different reliabilities or if more than two models are used.

primitives.name: Point differential dominance
primitives.verbatim_quote: If the predictions diverged, the team with the larger predicted point differential was deemed the predicted winner.
primitives.assumptions: Assumes that magnitude of predicted margin carries additional information beyond sign; assumes linear utility for point spreads; assumes no threshold effects.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Breaks down when point differentials are on vastly different scales; requires careful normalization or rescaling of disparate model outputs.

This chapter introduces foundational elements for forecasting college football outcomes by leveraging large-scale FBS game datasets spanning 2011–2016. It emphasizes the integration of box score statistics, point spreads, and recruiting data within a Bayesian and machine learning framework. The methodology begins with defining the scope of data volume, which includes 4,339 games, establishing a robust empirical basis for modeling. The augmentation of this dataset with composite team ratings from recruiting classes dating back to 2008 allows for capturing long-term trends in team development, particularly relevant for evaluating the impact of incoming classes on future performance. The process of creating training data cycles through annual iterations, where each team's data from 2011–2014 is used to predict outcomes in 2015, enables temporal consistency checks and validation of model generalization. To mitigate issues arising from repeated game instances in recompiled datasets, the paper proposes generating unique matchup numbers that encapsulate team-specific interactions. Covariates derived from recruiting data include relative differences in rankings and lagged performance metrics, enhancing the model’s ability to capture nuanced competitive dynamics. These primitives collectively support a probabilistic approach to forecasting, integrating both static and dynamic variables to improve predictive fidelity.
